title: The ten martyrs
hook: a Yom Kippur poem remembers ten sages killed by Rome

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rabbi Akiva said the Shema to the end and died on the word one. Your line was with all your soul. What did you do all the way through? Today, Akiva is remembered again, this time in a poem, with nine others. Day nine hundred five.

It's Yom Kippur. People have been fasting since the evening before. In the additional service, called Musaf, the room goes quiet for a long poem. It opens with two words in Hebrew, eleh ezkerah: these I remember. And then it tells, one by one, how Roman authorities put to death ten sages. The words echo a psalm: "These things I remember, and pour out my soul within me." On the Day of Atonement, in the middle of asking for forgiveness, the congregation stops to remember.
screen: `YOM KIPPUR, THE ADDITIONAL SERVICE.` → `ELEH EZKERAH: THESE I REMEMBER.` → `TEN SAGES, ONE BY ONE.`

segments.voice: The poem frames it as a single decree. A Roman ruler reads in the Torah that kidnapping a person and selling him is a crime punished by death, and he remembers that Joseph's brothers sold Joseph. Since the brothers are long gone, he demands ten sages in their place. Rabbi Yishmael, the poem says, purifies himself and ascends to heaven to ask whether this decree truly comes from above, and he is told to accept it. Then the names. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. Rabbi Yishmael. Rabbi Akiva, whose death we heard yesterday. Rabbi Chanina ben Teradion, who taught Torah in public with a scroll in his lap. The Talmud, in tractate Avodah Zarah, tells that he was burned wrapped in that scroll. His students asked what he saw, and he answered, in paraphrase: the parchment is burning, and the letters are flying up into the air. Some readers point out that the rabbis' own stories place these deaths in different times, not on one day. The poem gathers them anyway. It isn't a court record. It's a liturgy of memory, and it does what liturgy can do: it sets ten people in a row so a congregation can hold them together. A related lament is also said on the ninth of Av. And on Yom Kippur, the remembering sits inside the prayer, not beside it.
screen: `ONE DECREE, TEN SAGES.` · `RABBI YISHMAEL ASKS HEAVEN WHY.` · then, large: `THE PARCHMENT BURNS, THE LETTERS FLY.` · then: `THE POEM GATHERS THEM TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to remember people who died for their faith. Sit still and let your breath slow. Choose someone, from any time or place, who was killed for what they believed or for teaching it. You may know a name; you may only know a story. Say the name if you have one, quietly. If you only know where it happened, say that. Then rest with the image of letters rising: what they taught, still in the air. Don't hurry past them. If you pray, you can say a psalm you know in their memory. The bell holds the time.
Eleh ezkerah. These I remember, the Yom Kippur poem that names ten sages killed by Rome, among them Akiva and Chanina ben Teradion. Today's word.
Your line: the ten. Today, learn one name you didn't know of someone who suffered for their faith, and say it once aloud. Day nine hundred five.

howItsDone: In synagogues, the poem Eleh Ezkerah is read during the Yom Kippur Musaf service, and a related lament for the martyred sages is said on Tisha B'Av.

notes: Eleh Ezkerah paraphrased: the ruler's reading of the kidnapping law, the demand for ten sages, Rabbi Yishmael's ascent. Names given (Shimon ben Gamliel, Yishmael, Akiva, Chanina ben Teradion) follow the common order; please confirm.
'Some readers point out that the rabbis' own stories place these deaths in different times' — a scholarly claim; please confirm or soften.
howItsDone: the Tisha B'Av kinah (Arzei HaLevanon) is referred to as 'a related lament'; confirm.
Psalm 42 is KJV; the poem's opening 'eleh ezkerah' follows the Hebrew of Psalm 42:5.
Editor: Musaf is not 'late in the day', so the hook and screen were corrected; cut the stock 'the scroll can burn, the words go on' line (close to day 901's angle); practice opener varied.

Auditor (2026-10-01): Psalm 42:5 now quoted from JPS 1917 ('These things I remember...'), which keeps the Hebrew order eleh ezkerah the poem opens with; KJV had reversed it. Title corrected to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, as in the poem.
